issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette: Mr. Singh, a 64-year-old South Asian male, has been experiencing significant distress since his captivity experience two years ago. Married and working at a warehouse, Mr. Singh's life changed dramatically after the traumatic event that occurred one evening at around 8 PM. Since then, he has found himself in a cycle of fear and avoidance that has increasingly impacted both his work and personal life. At work, where the day shifts start late, the same time of day when the captivity began triggers intense anxiety for Mr. Singh. As the clock approaches 8 PM, he finds it difficult to concentrate on his tasks, often feeling as if the threat is looming again. This has led him to engage in maladaptive strategies such as avoiding sleep and frequently checking his surroundings for any signs of danger. The same time of day also evokes vivid memories of that evening, making it hard for him to function normally. One night, while watching a documentary about snakes on television, Mr. Singh was suddenly overwhelmed by the memory of encountering a snake during his captivity. This trigger has made him extremely anxious about any mention or visual representation of snakes, causing him to avoid watching TV programs and movies that might feature them. He is constantly vigilant, checking behind him and around corners, believing that he must remain hyperalert to prevent another traumatic event from occurring. Mr. Singh’s wife has noticed his distress and frequently finds herself reassuring him that he is safe at home, but even this does not seem to alleviate his anxiety. His constant body monitoring and reassurance-seeking behaviors have become a part of their daily routine. The fear of another attack has made Mr. Singh feel helpless and convinced that bad things are inevitable. He believes that if he thinks too much about the event, he will not be able to handle it, which further reinforces his avoidance behaviors. Mr. Singh’s nighttime vigilance is particularly troubling. Lying in bed at night, he constantly checks for signs of danger, making it difficult for him to fall asleep or remain asleep. His wife has observed that his sleep disturbances have become more frequent and severe over time. This lack of sleep exacerbates his anxiety, causing him to feel even less secure during the day. The experience of captivity has left Mr. Singh with a pervasive sense that life may not be worth living anymore. He often feels overwhelmed by the idea that he cannot prevent bad things from happening again. These negative appraisals have deepened his hypervigilance and reinforced his belief that the world is unsafe, particularly at night. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have compounded his distress. Mr. Singh’s constant checking for danger and avoidance of sleep have led to significant disruptions in his daily life. His relationship with his wife has also been strained as he relies heavily on her reassurances, which can feel burdensome for both of them. The cumulative effect of these behaviors has made it harder for him to engage in normal activities without feeling threatened or anxious. Mr. Singh finally sought help after realizing that his symptoms were worsening and affecting his ability to work and maintain a stable relationship with his wife. He is most afraid of the constant fear and vigilance that control his life, but he is also hopeful that through therapy, he can regain some sense of normalcy and feel more secure in his daily routines.
